cues.text: Let us turn now to the second chapter of this study session: building a strategic digital roadmap.
Before we look at the steps, let us be clear about what a roadmap is.
A roadmap is the bridge between where an organisation wants to go and the actions it will actually take to get there.
In digital transformation, it is how a strategy becomes a sequence of concrete decisions, rather than a collection of good intentions.
The source gives us a process of seven steps, and the order matters, so let us walk through them one at a time.
Step one: define the business vision and desired outcomes.
Everything begins with the question, what are we trying to achieve for the business?
Without a clear vision and outcomes, technology choices have nothing to be measured against.
Step two: assess current maturity, infrastructure, processes, skills, customer pain points and data.
Here the organisation looks honestly at where it stands today.
That means its digital maturity, the infrastructure it runs on, the processes it follows, the skills its people have, the pain points its customers experience, and the data it holds.
You cannot plan a route without knowing your starting point.
Step three: analyse competitors and emerging opportunities.
The organisation looks outward, at what competitors are doing and at new opportunities that are appearing in the market.
Step four: identify gaps and prioritise initiatives by value, risk, feasibility and dependencies.
Now we compare where we are with where we want to be.
The differences are the gaps.

We cannot close every gap at once, so we rank initiatives using four lenses: the value they create, the risk they carry, how feasible they are, and what dependencies they have, meaning what must be in place before they can succeed.
Step five: develop the target architecture, operating model and capability plan.

The organisation designs what the future state looks like: the technology architecture, the operating model describing how work and responsibilities are organised, and the plan for building the capabilities required.
Step six: assign resources, milestones, accountable owners and governance.
Plans fail when nobody owns them.
So this step gives each initiative its resources, its milestones, a named person who is accountable, and the governance structure that oversees progress and decisions.
Step seven: pilot, measure, scale and revise as evidence changes.
The organisation starts with a pilot, measures what happens, scales what works, and revises the plan as new evidence arrives.
Notice that the roadmap is not fixed forever.
It adapts to evidence.
Now, an important point.
A roadmap translates strategy into sequenced actions; it is not just a deadline list.
A list of dates tells you when things happen.
A roadmap tells you what happens, in what order, why that order, and how it connects to the strategy.
A good roadmap uses SMART objectives.
SMART is an acronym.
The objective should be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Let us look at the example in the source: reduce median loan processing from five days to one day within six months while maintaining fraud-loss and compliance limits.
Test it against each letter.
It is specific, because it concerns loan processing.
It is measurable, because we use the median processing time, moving from five days to one day.
It has a time bound, which is six months.
And it carries guardrails: fraud losses and compliance limits must be maintained.
That last part is very important.
It means the speed gain cannot be achieved by weakening controls.
Now let us separate two ideas that students often confuse: milestones and benefits.
The source gives this example of a milestone: validated digital identity integration.
This is a meaningful step.
It enables the objective, because faster loan processing may depend on verifying customers digitally.
But, as the source states, it is not itself the benefit.
The benefit is the outcome the customer and the business experience, in this case faster loan processing within the stated limits.
Completing a milestone shows progress; it does not prove that value has been delivered.
Next, how do we prioritise when we have many possible projects?
The source offers a weighted scoring approach.
The criteria and weights are these: strategic alignment, forty percent; customer benefit, thirty percent; feasibility, twenty percent; and risk acceptability, ten percent.
Together these add up to one hundred percent.
Let us work through the source example.
A project is scored five, four, three and four out of five, in that same order of criteria.
So strategic alignment scores five, customer benefit scores four, feasibility scores three, and risk acceptability scores four.
Now multiply each score by its weight.
Strategic alignment: five times point four equals two.
Customer benefit: four times point three equals one point two.
Feasibility: three times point two equals point six.
Risk acceptability: four times point one equals point four.
Add them together: two plus one point two plus point six plus point four equals four point two.
So the project's weighted score is four point two out of five.
But a score on its own means little.
The source tells us to compare it against alternatives, because the number only helps when set beside other candidate projects.
And it adds a crucial safeguard: mandatory risk constraints must be met separately.
In other words, certain requirements are pass or fail conditions, not points to be traded off.
As the source says, a high average cannot compensate for an unlawful design.
A project that scores four point two but breaks the law is not a good project; it must not proceed in that form.
Finally, let us look at an example from industry.
The source uses Amazon as a teaching example.
It illustrates an evolution beyond online retail into cloud services, subscriptions, logistics and data-driven personalisation.
Notice the pattern: Amazon did not simply stay as an online shop.
Its roadmap links customer value and reusable capabilities to new offerings.
A capability built for one purpose, such as logistics or data handling, can be reused to support new services.
The lesson here is a warning.
Copying the visible product without the underlying capabilities and governance is not a strategy.
Seeing a successful subscription or cloud offering and imitating only that surface is not enough.
What made it work was the foundation beneath it: the capabilities, and the governance that directs them.
A real roadmap builds those foundations deliberately, in sequence, and ties them to customer value.
To bring the chapter together: begin with vision, assess honestly, look outward, prioritise carefully, design the future state, assign ownership, and then pilot, measure, scale and revise.

Keep objectives SMART, do not confuse milestones with benefits, score projects transparently while treating legal and risk constraints as non-negotiable, and build real capabilities rather than copying surface features.
